transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 14:00 - 14:46 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Sarah (MapleCare Dir ML), Tom (MapleCare Eng Mg), Priya (MapleCare Security), Evan (MapleCare DS)

Summary: weekly POC check-in to review quality evals and regression checks on prompt sets. Discussed recent drop in NER recall on insurance forms, guardrail tuning to reduce hallucinations, and next steps for a dedicated latency run.

Topics:
- Current quality metrics (intent accuracy, NER precision/recall)
- Prompt-set regressions and failure triage
- Guardrails & content filters (safety thresholding)
- Deployment mode tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated / VPC)
- Action items and timeline for pilot progression

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: all right everyone, thanks for joining. quick check-in, we'll go through the latest quality report, triage the failures, and decide next steps. sound good?
[00:09] Sarah: yep, sounds good. we had the team look at the new evals you sent, thanks for that. saw a noticeable drop in NER recall on the insurance form dataset.
[00:18] Diego: yeah i pulled that up — the recall dropped from about 0.86 to 0.78 after we moved to the newer prompt template that constrains tokens, probably due to shorter context windows and the new truncation strategy.
[00:30] Tom: i wonder if it's tokenization or the kv cash — sorry, kv cache behavior when we chunk long docs. some entities are getting split across chunk boundaries and then missed.
[00:45] Diego: good call, we did see some boundary artifacts. that's the KV cache interaction with our chunking heuristics. we can tweak the overlap size to keep entities intact; increasing overlap from 50 to 120 tokens fixed ~60% of those misses in my local runs.
[01:05] Evan: show the numbers?
[01:07] Diego: sure, on the 1k test set: baseline (old prompt) F1 0.84 / recall 0.86. new prompt F1 0.79 / recall 0.78. with overlap 120 -> F1 0.83 / recall 0.85. cost delta small, tokens +3%.
[01:27] Sarah: ok that's promising. would prefer not to increase tokens much since cost is a concern for us. what about prompt engineering — can we add explicit entity anchors?
[01:38] Maya: we already tried adding anchors in 3a and 3b prompt sets; anchors help precision but they can lower recall if the model is too literal. Diego, results on anchor variants?
[01:49] Diego: variant 3b with anchors improved precision from 0.88 to 0.91 but recall dipped to 0.75 in that run. so anchors help filter false positives but lose fuzzy matches.
[02:03] Tom: sounds like a tradeoff: precision vs recall vs cost. can we do hybrid — anchors plus a softer similarity pass?
[02:12] Diego: yeah we prototyped a two-step pipeline: initial extraction with anchor-biased prompt (high precision) then a second pass focused on low-confidence spans with a looser prompt. that recovered recall to 0.83 and precision 0.89. latency increased ~60ms per request on average.
[02:33] Priya: from security perspective, any two-pass approach increases request surface and logs. we need to confirm data residency and audit logging — also how partial responses are cached. we have SOC two and HIPAA concerns.
[02:47] Maya: understood. we'll include the compliance impact in the tradeoff doc and the CSM will follow up. Lena, can you take point on logging implications?
[02:55] Lena: yep will do.
[02:57] [03:00] Sarah: another regression we spotted: in the summarization microtask we saw more hallucinations around provider names — model invents a clinic. Looks like temperature or sampling issue?
[03:11] Diego: we fixed decoding to greedy in recent config to reduce hallucinations, but there were still a few cases. many were due to prompt ambiguity where the prompt didn't explicitly say "only use names present in the source." adding that guardrail cut hallucinations by ~70% in our tests.
[03:28] Evan: can you show example?
[03:30] Diego: yep — original prompt: "summarize the visit notes." new guardrail: "summarize the visit notes using only the information in the notes; do not add or invent names, providers, or diagnoses." output after guardrail matched ground truth more often.
[03:48] Tom: good, we should add those as canonical rules in the prompt library so they don't regressed in the next rollout.
[03:55] Maya: agreed. we'll version the prompt set and add a rule that any new prompt must include explicit hallucination guardrails where appropriate.
[04:05] [04:10] Sarah: about scoring — your scorecards showed overall intent accuracy 92% but NER recall was the outlier. how are you weighting metrics for the pilot?
[04:20] Maya: for this pilot we suggested a composite score: 50% task accuracy (intent/QA), 30% NER F1, 20% hallucination rate (lower is better). we can tweak weights based on your business priorities.
[04:33] Sarah: can we bump NER to 40%? that's most product-critical.
[04:37] Maya: sure, we'll update the dashboard weighting and re-rank the model variants accordingly.
[04:44] [05:00] Evan: question on test sets — our prod mirror has some PII that we can't share. can we run the 1k holdout on our side and send redacted failures?
[05:09] Priya: yes and we need to confirm encryption-at-rest and KMS key access for any logs shared.
[05:16] Maya: understood. Redwood supports customer-managed KMS in Private mode and logs can be restricted. we'll send the compliance packing and a short note on how logs are redacted in Hosted.
[05:27] [06:00] Diego: on the model side, we ran a quantized variant (int8-ish) that reduced token cost by ~38% and latency by 12ms avg. quality delta was small on intent (~<1%) but slightly worse on rare-entity recall (~3% drop).
[06:19] Tom: that's notable. could the recall drop be exacerbated by the quantization + chunk boundary issue?
[06:26] Diego: yeah both interact. quantization can reduce sensitivity to rare tokens which hurts entity recognition. we can try targeted higher-precision kernels for the NER-head or larger context window only for NER passes.
[06:40] Sarah: that might be acceptable if cost savings are big — need to see end-to-end numbers.
[06:45] Maya: Diego will run an eval that mixes quantized generation for general tasks and a non-quantized NER pass for the critical extraction spans.
[06:55] [07:00] Evan: for regression detection — how are we monitoring drift? some weekly plots would help.
[07:07] Diego: we pushed a small dashboard showing per-prompt and per-model metrics with statistical tests (bootstrap) to flag regressions beyond a 2% threshold. currently it's manual review but we can add auto-alerts.
[07:20] Sarah: add auto-alerts please, we don't want regressions slipping.
[07:23] Lena: we'll put alerts into the console; need to confirm who gets paged.
[07:28] [07:40] Priya: also please document retention period for debug tokens and provide an option to scrub PII.
[07:46] Maya: yes, we'll include that in the compliance doc.
[07:50] [08:00] Tom: question on deployment modes — you mentioned dedicated GPUs earlier. how many GPUs for our target 200 RPS baseline?
[08:09] Diego: rough ballpark: with batching and the model we tested, about 6-8 A100-equivalent GPUs in Dedicated would meet 200 RPS with p95 latency ~320ms. Hosted will autoscale but Dedicated gives better predictability and isolation.
[08:26] Sarah: cost estimate?
[08:28] Maya: we'll send a dedicated vs hosted cost breakdown after Diego completes the quantized mixed-run and we produce token-level cost numbers.
[08:36] [09:00] Evan: on the prompt library, can you surface the failing prompts and the exact input that triggered the failure? it's easier to triage with the original tokens.
[09:09] Diego: yes we can include failure traces with tokenized inputs and model logits redacted if needed. we'll make sure PII is masked.
[09:20] [09:30] Sarah: one more ask — can we get a short writeup on fallback policies? when the primary model misses, we'd like an automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant rather than serve degraded content.
[09:39] Maya: Redwood supports policy-based routing: fallback by latency tier or quality tier. we'll propose a policy that triggers fallback for inputs with low-confidence scores or when p95 latency spikes.
[09:51] Tom: how do we compute low-confidence? is it entropy-based?
[09:55] Diego: we use a mix: token-level perplexity and calibrated confidence from a small head. combines to a single confidence score. thresholding is tunable per-route.
[10:08] [10:30] Maya: recap and next steps: Diego will run mixed quant/non-quant eval and share numbers (due 3/8); Maya to push updated prompt set and versioned library with guardrails (due 3/6); Evan to run 1k holdout and send failures (due 3/11); Lena to collate compliance Qs and follow up on logging (due 3/10). we'll also schedule the Dedicated latency benchmarking session for 3/9.
[10:54] Sarah: that works. thanks everyone.
[11:00] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts and invite for the 3/9 run.
[11:06] End of call.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker chops and minor mis-heard technical terms ("kv cash" instead of KV cache; "SOC two" spelled out).
